## Responses as Code

Each turn, you take your turn by calling the `submit_program` tool. Its `program`
string is run as one Ruby program: pass one whole, legal
Ruby program — bare code, with no code fences around it and no
prose inside it — and it is processed exactly as written. All calls are
synchronous.

`submit_program` is the only tool in this session, and every reply must call it.
Each call is acknowledged with a tool result reading `ok`; what the program
produced arrives as separate messages after it. Text you write alongside the
call is recorded, but nothing reads code out of it: only the `program` string
runs. If one reply makes several `submit_program` calls, the programs run
sequentially, in order, every one of them.

Your program is compiled by `opal` before it runs. A program it refuses
is not executed: you get its diagnostics and submit another program.

## Views

Views are the only way to read data out of your code and are provided on the
turn after they're opened. Print statements are not shown.

Reading images is not supported.

## Language Rules

Your program is executed exactly as you wrote it, as the whole of a `program.rb`,
at its top level.

## Ending your session

Turns continue until you end your session.

A program that fails does not end your session: the ending it called is revoked.
Fix the fault and end your session in a program that runs to completion.

Call `GG::Session.finish` with a short summary of what you did once the work is
complete.

## Your modules

Your program is given these modules:

- `GG::Docs`: Find what the agent can call, and take a documentation view back out of the window. — brought into scope with `require "gg"`
- `GG::Files`: Read, write, edit and list the files of the workspace. — brought into scope with `require "gg"`
- `GG::Shell`: Run shell commands in the workspace. — brought into scope with `require "gg"`
- `GG::Views`: Show a file, a computed value, or a module, function or type's documentation. — brought into scope with `require "gg"`
- `GG::Session`: End the session, with the ending that belongs to this agent's role. — brought into scope with `require "gg"`

Search the documentation to find a function, by keyword or by naming modules
above. Open a documentation view of each function you intend to call, and write
the call on a later turn.

The SDK declares every function, whatever this run enabled, so a call to one this
run withheld compiles and then fails when it runs, naming the call. What you can
find in the documentation is what you can call.

## Messages you receive

Every message you receive is headed by one of the following labels, on its own
line — a view's label is followed by `: ` and the name it was opened under; a
file view's by `: `, its path, `:`, the 1-based inclusive line range shown and
the file's total line count — followed by a `----` rule and then the content:

- `Task` — the task you are working on, or a message from a parent agent
- `Compiler error` — your last program did not compile, so none of it ran; the message is the compiler's error and nothing else. Fix it and resend the whole program
- `Runtime error` — your last program compiled and then threw, or was stopped by a sandbox limit; the message is the error and nothing else. Whatever the program did before it threw stands, so do not repeat that work
- `Notice` — a process notice from the harness (a mode change, or guidance)
- `Summary` — a summary standing in for older turns the harness compacted out of the window
- `Documentation` — documentation or a skill you asked to read, delivered on the following turn

For example, lines 100 to 250 of a 400-line file you opened a view of arrive
as:

```
File: src/main.ts:100-250 of 400 lines
----
...those lines of the file...
```

A program that ran is not announced: the views it opened are the result.

  modules?: Array<String> = [] (passed by name) — The modules to look in, each named by its gg id — `files`, `views`, `docs` — or by the path a program writes it as, `GG::Files`, and matched exactly. Documentation: GG::Core::ApiError
----
class ApiError < StandardError
  attr_reader operation: String
  attr_reader code: Symbol
end

Defined in `GG::Core`, brought into scope with `require "gg"`.

A gg call that failed.

Every function in this SDK raises one of these rather than returning a status, which is what a Ruby author expects of a library and what makes a failure compose: a program that rescues nothing ends on the raise, and gg is told which call failed and on which line. It is a `StandardError`, so a bare `rescue => failure` catches it too.

A failure a program expects is an ordinary `rescue` branching on `code`:

```ruby
begin
  GG::Views.open_text("build log", log)
rescue GG::Core::ApiError => failure
  raise unless failure.code == GG::Core::ApiErrorCode::LIMIT_EXCEEDED

  GG::Views.open_text("build log (tail)", log[-40_000..])
end
```
  operation: String — The call that failed, by the key of the operation the program reached for (`read_file`, `spawn_subagent`).

It is gg's key rather than this SDK's method name, so it is the same string on every language a program may be written in.
  code: Symbol — The failure class, so a rescue branches on a value rather than on prose. One of `GG::Core::ApiErrorCode`'s symbols.

Documentation: GG::Views.open_file
----
open_file(path, offset: nil, limit: nil, max_line_chars: nil) -> GG::Files::TextFile or GG::Files::ImageFile
  path: String — The file to open, relative to the workspace or absolute.
  offset?: Integer or nil = nil (passed by name) — The 1-based line to start at.
  limit?: Integer or nil = nil (passed by name) — How many lines to show from `offset`.
  max_line_chars?: Integer or nil = nil (passed by name) — The most characters of each line to show, 1 to 65,536; a longer line is cut there and annotated with how many characters were dropped. Leave it out to show lines whole.

Defined in `GG::Views`, brought into scope with `require "gg"`.

Read a file and place it in the context window, attributed to its path and filed under it.

What comes back is exactly what `GG::Files.read_file` returns; the difference is the view. That split is the point: reading gets bytes for the program, opening shows the file to the agent, so a program that reads forty files to grep them puts nothing in the window. `offset` and `limit` select a window of lines, and two pages of one file are two views that coexist; re-opening the same page replaces what it showed rather than piling up a duplicate. An image is shown as a picture, and this is the only call that shows one.

Re-opening a picture that is already open replaces it rather than adding a second copy, which is the same rule a page of a file follows.

The view's text body is held to the same 65,536-byte cap a `GG::Views.open_text` body is: a window that would carry more is refused, naming the size and the bound, and nothing is opened — never a truncation. The way out is a narrower window, with `offset` and `limit`, or `max_line_chars`, which cuts each line of the view longer than that many characters at that point and annotates it in place as `foo (123 more chars...)`, with the count of characters dropped. The cut is the view's alone — what this call returns and the file itself are untouched — and the byte cap is measured against the body after it, which is what lets a window over a log of enormous lines fit. Left out, lines arrive whole. A picture is not a text body and is not subject to the cap.

Returns: the same thing `GG::Files.read_file` returns

Raises `GG::Core::ApiError`: `:not_found` for a missing path, `:invalid_argument` for an offset past the end of the file or a `max_line_chars` of zero or over 65,536, and `:limit_exceeded` — naming the size and the bound — for a text window over the cap. The read is what fails; nothing is opened when it does.

# Inventory brief

Write `notes/inventory.md` describing the workspace root.

## Required content

1. A top-level heading reading `# Workspace inventory`.
2. One Markdown list entry per entry of the workspace's top-level
   directory, in the order the listing returns them.
3. Each entry formatted as `- `, the entry's name, then ` (dir)` for a
   directory or ` (file)` for a file.

## Rules

- List the top-level directory only; do not recurse.
- Create the `notes/` directory as part of the write if it does not exist.
- Change nothing else in the workspace.

## Responses as Code

Each turn, you take your turn by calling the `submit_program` tool. Its `program`
string is run as one Ruby program: pass one whole, legal
Ruby program — bare code, with no code fences around it and no
prose inside it — and it is processed exactly as written. All calls are
synchronous.

`submit_program` is the only tool in this session, and every reply must call it.
Each call is acknowledged with a tool result reading `ok`; what the program
produced arrives as separate messages after it. Text you write alongside the
call is recorded, but nothing reads code out of it: only the `program` string
runs. If one reply makes several `submit_program` calls, the programs run
sequentially, in order, every one of them.

Your program is compiled by `opal` before it runs. A program it refuses
is not executed: you get its diagnostics and submit another program.

## Views

Views are the only way to read data out of your code and are provided on the
turn after they're opened. Print statements are not shown.

Reading images is not supported.

## Language Rules

Your program is executed exactly as you wrote it, as the whole of a `program.rb`,
at its top level.

## Ending your session

Turns continue until you end your session.

A program that fails does not end your session: the ending it called is revoked.
Fix the fault and end your session in a program that runs to completion.

Call `GG::Session.finish` with a short summary of what you did once the work is
complete.

## Your modules

Your program is given these modules:

- `GG::Docs`: Find what the agent can call, and take a documentation view back out of the window. — brought into scope with `require "gg"`
- `GG::Files`: Read, write, edit and list the files of the workspace. — brought into scope with `require "gg"`
- `GG::Shell`: Run shell commands in the workspace. — brought into scope with `require "gg"`
- `GG::Views`: Show a file, a computed value, or a module, function or type's documentation. — brought into scope with `require "gg"`
- `GG::Session`: End the session, with the ending that belongs to this agent's role. — brought into scope with `require "gg"`

Search the documentation to find a function, by keyword or by naming modules
above. Open a documentation view of each function you intend to call, and write
the call on a later turn.

The SDK declares every function, whatever this run enabled, so a call to one this
run withheld compiles and then fails when it runs, naming the call. What you can
find in the documentation is what you can call.

Every message you receive is headed by one of the following labels, on its own
line — a view's label is followed by `: ` and the name it was opened under; a
file view's by `: `, its path, `:`, the 1-based inclusive line range shown and
the file's total line count — followed by a `----` rule and then the content:

- `Compiler error` — your last program did not compile, so none of it ran; the message is the compiler's error and nothing else. Fix it and resend the whole program
- `Runtime error` — your last program compiled and then threw, or was stopped by a sandbox limit; the message is the error and nothing else. Whatever the program did before it threw stands, so do not repeat that work

Read a file and place it in the context window, attributed to its path and filed under it.

What comes back is exactly what `GG::Files.read_file` returns; the difference is the view. That split is the point: reading gets bytes for the program, opening shows the file to the agent, so a program that reads forty files to grep them puts nothing in the window. `offset` and `limit` select a window of lines, and two pages of one file are two views that coexist; re-opening the same page replaces what it showed rather than piling up a duplicate. An image is shown as a picture, and this is the only call that shows one.

Re-opening a picture that is already open replaces it rather than adding a second copy, which is the same rule a page of a file follows.

The view's text body is held to the same 65,536-byte cap a `GG::Views.open_text` body is: a window that would carry more is refused, naming the size and the bound, and nothing is opened — never a truncation. The way out is a narrower window, with `offset` and `limit`, or `max_line_chars`, which cuts each line of the view longer than that many characters at that point and annotates it in place as `foo (123 more chars...)`, with the count of characters dropped. The cut is the view's alone — what this call returns and the file itself are untouched — and the byte cap is measured against the body after it, which is what lets a window over a log of enormous lines fit. Left out, lines arrive whole. A picture is not a text body and is not subject to the cap.

The read is what fails; nothing is opened when it does.
